title: He Renamed Himself After Matisse. The Whitney Still Wouldn't Call Him American.
standfirst: Walasse Ting invented an artist's name that echoed Henri Matisse and spent two decades repainting, from memory, the birds he found at a Miami wildlife park. Curators on both continents kept deciding what he wasn't — not Chinese enough, not American enough — and his first full U.S. museum retrospective didn't open until thirteen years after he died.

sections.heading: The Park Behind Every Parrot He Ever Painted
sections.body: Walasse Ting's in-laws lived in South Florida, and through the 1980s his yearly visits to see them always included a stop at [Parrot Jungle](https://nsuartmuseum.org/exhibition/walasse-ting-parrot-jungle/), the wildlife park that had stood in Pinecrest since Francis and Louise Scherr opened it in December 1936. He photographed and sketched what he found there — macaws, cockatoos, flamingos — by the hundred, then carried the pictures home and repainted them from memory in a New York studio, unconcerned with rendering the animals "as they were" and loyal only to how they looked once his own colour had got hold of them. One critic reviewing the resulting body of work called it, flatly, ["the fullest realization of Ting's singular style."](https://bocamag.com/museums-walasse-ting-show-an-ode-to-parrot-jungle-and-beyond/) *Blue Lady with Parrots*, made in 2000, sits at the tail end of that habit — a son-in-law's day trip turned, over twenty years, into a private aviary he could repaint at will.

sections.heading: A Name Spelled to Rhyme With Matisse
sections.body: When Ting arrived in Paris in the early 1950s, he stopped using the name he had been given in Wuxi and began signing his work Walasse — spelled, according to more than one account of his life, to echo Matisse rather than the more obvious "Wallace." He adopted it only a year or two before [Matisse died, in 1954](https://www.1stdibs.com/introspective-magazine/walasse-ting), as though quietly positioning himself as the old man's successor while the old man was still there to notice. The accounts do not fully agree: one source has the same sound doubling as a childhood nickname meaning something closer to "spoiled." Both can be true of a man who spent the rest of his career resisting a single tidy story. What nobody disputes is the nerve in it — a newly arrived, largely self-taught painter from Shanghai, broke enough to be washing cars for francs at a Paris garage, chose to spell his new name after the most famous colourist alive in Europe. French customers at that garage called him Charlie, a condescending catch-all some of them used for any Chinese man, and by one account he simply laughed it off.

sections.heading: Hundreds of Paintings Signed by Two Men
sections.body: In Paris, Ting grew close to painters who had belonged to [CoBrA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COBRA_%28art_movement%29) — Karel Appel, Asger Jorn and, closest of all, Pierre Alechinsky. The alliance of Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam painters, which had prized instinct over any inherited grammar of painting, was already formally dissolved by the time Ting reached France, but its former members kept working in that spirit for years afterward, and Ting worked alongside them. He and Alechinsky produced hundreds of joint paintings the two of them nicknamed "Alechings," collaborations energetic enough that neither man's hand is easy to separate from the other's on the finished sheet. The friendship ran in both directions: Ting turned Alechinsky toward acrylic paint, and separately introduced the American minimalist Dan Flavin to Japanese ink — an artist who kept moving information between circles that otherwise had little reason to talk to each other.

sections.heading: A Portfolio That Made Warhol Share a Page With Him
sections.body: Ting's other landmark project used no paint at all. In 1964 the Swiss dealer Eberhard Kornfeld published *1¢ Life*, a portfolio of lithographs — the count runs to 61 or 62 depending on the source — by twenty-eight contemporary artists, its costs underwritten in part by the Detroit collector Florence Barron. Ting supplied the poems that ran alongside the pictures and assembled much of the roster himself: Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein, Joan Mitchell, Robert Rauschenberg, Claes Oldenburg, and his old Paris friends Alechinsky, Appel and Jorn all contributed, alongside his close friend [Sam Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Francis). One assessment of Ting's own poetry called it "stripped-down, billboard-like English," closer to advertising copy than to verse in the expected sense: "parent love children as summer garden hold tree / husband love wife as long distance call / husband love mistress as rainbow in pocket / girl love man as open dream," from a piece titled "All Kinds of Love." A separate poem, "Black Stone," was dedicated to Francis and reads, in Ting's own capitals: "WHO SAY NO BEAUTY IN THIS WORLD / WHO SAY NO TRUTH ON EARTH."

sections.heading: Filed Under Fauvism, Claimed by No One
sections.body: The database behind this feature files *Blue Lady with Parrots* under Fauvism, a movement that ran from roughly 1904 to 1908 and belonged to painters two generations older than Ting, working in a Paris he would not reach for another four decades. The label is not exactly wrong, though — it is an echo of the name he chose for himself, not of anything he actually painted; his real debts ran to CoBrA's improvisation, to Pop's flat outline, to Chinese brush and ink. Nobody ever let him settle on one box. [Ariella Wolens](https://u.osu.edu/mclc/2025/05/19/walasse-ting/), who curated his first full American museum retrospective, put the trouble plainly: "he wasn't Chinese enough for the Chinese or American enough for the Americans." His daughter, Mia, has said something close to the same thing in her own way — "I don't think he felt at home anywhere." She has also given the sharper version: ["The Whitney did not consider him an American artist,"](https://www.1stdibs.com/introspective-magazine/walasse-ting) she says. "He got very upset over that." Ting seems to have arrived at the same verdict himself: one of his own poems is titled "Walasse Ting on Walasse Ting," and states its subject's position as flatly as a label on a museum wall — "individual, not belonging to any group."

sections.heading: Both Endings Landed in the Same Year
sections.body: Ting suffered a stroke in 2002, after which, by every account, he never painted again; he died of a cerebral hemorrhage in Manhattan on 17 May 2010, at eighty-one. That same year, the Pinecrest site of Parrot Jungle — the park he had been visiting since the 1980s, the one behind *Blue Lady with Parrots* and everything like it — was sold for redevelopment. The attraction [reopened on Miami's Watson Island the following year and dropped "Parrot" from its name for good in 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungle_Island). Neither the man nor the place he had quietly been repainting for two decades survived intact past 2002. Recognition, when it came, came late: Ting's first full monographic museum show in the United States, *Walasse Ting: Parrot Jungle*, opened at Fort Lauderdale's NSU Art Museum on 10 November 2023 — thirteen years after he died, and decades after his own first yearly trip to the park it was named for.
